Chapter 4: Distinguishing God’s Voice from Other Influences
Let’s take a moment to talk about something that can feel a little tricky—knowing when a thought or feeling is truly from God, or just coming from somewhere else. If you’ve ever asked yourself, “Is this really inspiration, or just my own idea?”—you’re not alone. Our minds are busy places, full of emotions, opinions, and all sorts of outside pressures. Learning to sort out what’s divine from what’s not? That’s a skill, and honestly, it takes time, self-awareness, and a bit of spiritual tuning.
So, how do you actually start telling the difference? Well, one thing that helps is understanding what God’s voice tends to sound like. Usually, it’s calm. Gentle. Uplifting. It guides you toward growth, brings a sense of peace, and lines up with love and truth. If the message you’re feeling is harsh, anxious, or just focused on your own interests, chances are, it’s not coming from God.
In Christian belief, the Holy Ghost is considered the main way God communicates with us. You might’ve heard it called the “still, small voice”—that quiet nudge that brings clarity and reassurance. It’s nothing like a fleeting emotion or a random thought that pops in and out of your head.
Now, if you’re wondering how to get better at this, here are a few practical things you can try:
First, pause and reflect. Instead of jumping to act on every feeling, take a moment to think it through. This gives you a chance to clear away impulsive emotions and see what’s really there.
Second, compare your impressions with scripture. If what you’re feeling lines up with the teachings you find in scripture or with Christ’s example, it’s a good sign that you’re on the right track.
Third, seek confirmation. If you find the same impression keeps returning, you feel a sense of peace about it, or you get outside confirmation—maybe from a trusted friend or mentor—that can help you feel more confident about the guidance you’re receiving.
Another thing to watch for: genuine revelation usually bears good fruit. It leads to more love, patience, humility, and a desire to serve others.
And finally, be careful with extremes. If you feel pressured to make a sudden, drastic decision out of fear or pride, it’s worth slowing down and checking in with yourself.
Here’s a helpful way to picture it: tuning a radio. There are lots of stations out there, but with some careful adjustment, you find the one you really want. Spiritual discernment works the same way. You have to filter out all the noise—distractions, fears, and your own biases—to hear that quiet, steady voice of the Spirit.
Think about this—maybe you’ve had a moment where you felt like you needed to act quickly, but after taking a breath, you realized it was just anxiety talking. Or maybe you kept feeling a gentle urge to check in on a friend, and when you did, it led to a really meaningful conversation. Those real-life moments are where discernment really matters.
The truth is, discernment isn’t something you master overnight. It’s a lifelong practice that takes humility, a willingness to learn, and a real desire to line your life up with what’s true. Over time, you’ll start to recognize the difference between God’s voice and all the other influences out there—and as you do, you’ll find more confidence in following that guidance, even when things feel uncertain.
